column3: It directly joins disbelief in Allah's signs to the objection that reduced bones and fragments cannot be raised anew.
The question whether the first ancestors are included preserves the ancestral dimension of the focus's objection.
It closely states the claimed impossibility: after death, dust, and bones, people will be brought forth.
The same dust-and-bones question confirms the collective form of the denial, though its substance is already established.
The next ayah develops the focus locally: the promised return of the speakers and their fathers is dismissed as ancient tales.
Bringing a people from darkness to light gives only a distant sense of divine deliverance, not resurrection from dust.
Its objection to being raised from bones and fragments reinforces the material basis of resurrection denial.
Divine bounty and human ingratitude do not clarify the objection to postmortem emergence.
Rules for divorce and leaving homes use a different kind of departure from the focus's being brought forth.
The terse question about decayed bones supplies a reduced but redundant form of the bodily objection.
The nearby charge of madness frames rejection of truth but adds no resurrection-specific content.
Emergence from the body concerns generation, not return after death.

Reviving a dead land through measured rain and saying people will likewise be brought forth supplies a direct natural analogy.

The approach of the true promise and disbelievers' awakened regret provide general end-time context.

The earth bringing forth water and pasture offers only a limited emergence image.

Joseph's release from prison and reunion with parents use a different sense of being brought out.

Expulsion from Medina concerns social status, not resurrection.

The conspirators' plan to kill at night is unrelated to emergence from dust.
Divine power to bring living from dead and dead from living offers a creation-and-life basis for challenging the objection.
The damned seeking revenge on their misleaders does not clarify resurrection.

The local command to inspect the fate of sinners supplies the warning surrounding the skeptics' demand.
Dust on a rock in an almsgiving parable does not concern return from dust.
The arrogant group's explicit disbelief gives a general social form of rejection without resurrection content.
Moses's staff and flight do not explain the focus.
Being brought forth as a community for people concerns moral mission, not resurrection.

The appeal to fathers' worship shows ancestral resistance but no claim about postmortem return.
The prohibition on expelling people from their homes is unrelated to being raised from earth.
Calling the guidance an old fabrication parallels dismissal of revelation but not the material objection.
The local creation of gardens by rain points generally to divine creative power without stating resurrection.
Humanity's creation from dust into spreading people directly challenges treating dust as incapable of yielding life.
Calling the Quran a fabrication is a general rejection of the message, not return from death.
The distinction between the people of Fire and Paradise adds no account of resurrection.
Bringing grain and vegetation from the earth offers a secondary analogy of hidden matter becoming visible.
The chiefs' accusation of clear error does not concern resurrection.
Solomon's death and the jinn's ignorance of the unseen do not explain being brought forth after death.
The repeated death-dust-bones objection adds the consequence of being held to account, though the formula is already covered.

Pharaoh's claim of being expelled from the land uses a different sense of removal.

Matched companions in Paradise do not clarify resurrection.

The marital exception has no relation to the focus.
Threatening Lot with expulsion is unrelated to postmortem emergence.
The bare statement that disbelievers persist in denial adds no specific content.
Adam's creation from dust supplies a distinct origin-from-dust basis for the possibility of re-creation.
The claim that Moses seeks to expel people from their land is not resurrection.
The image of disbelievers rushing toward the Prophet gives only a general oppositional setting.
Continuing ancestral worship illustrates inherited practice but not denial that ancestors can be raised.
The extraction from gardens and springs is a historical displacement, not emergence after death.
The general assertion that disbelievers deny gives no incremental explanation.
The inhabited House does not concern the focus's denial.
Leaving a home for battle is unrelated to resurrection.

Expelling Lot's family from a town is a different kind of removal.

God bringing hidden hypocrisy to light is not postmortem emergence.

Bringing out daylight is unrelated to resurrection from dust.
Noah's instruction to board the ark does not clarify the focus.
Expulsion of believers from their homes concerns persecution, not bodily return.

Rules of modesty and family relations do not concern resurrection.

Differences in provision and denial of blessing do not clarify return from dust.
Paradisal clothing and drink add no account of resurrection's possibility.

God's reviving of the dead is presented as a sign, furnishing a concrete counterexample to disbelief in return to life.
The revivified birds provide an enacted demonstration that dispersed bodily matter can be summoned back.
The disbelievers' assertion that there is only worldly life and no resurrection supplies the broader denial without the dust imagery.
Its statement that God will raise the dead directly answers the claimed impossibility, though without the focus's ancestral formulation.
Humanity lives, dies, and is brought forth from the earth, closely matching the focus's movement from dust to emergence.

God originates creation and then repeats it, establishing the same creation-and-return logic as the local answer in 27:64.

It records the emphatic claim that God will not raise the dead and answers it as God's binding promise.
The reply identifies the original Creator as the one who will restore reduced bones, directly completing the objection in 17:49.
The human question whether he will be brought forth alive after death closely restates the focus's central challenge.
Remembering creation from nothing directly rebuts the inference that death prevents renewed life.
It states that people are made from earth, returned to it, and brought forth from it once more.
Folding creation and repeating it as it began supplies a comprehensive creation-to-recreation frame.

God gives life to the dead and has power over all things, providing the doctrinal answer to the material objection.
It explicitly affirms that God will raise those in the graves when the inevitable Hour comes.
It places death after earthly life, preparing the precise sequel that resurrection follows it.
It explicitly says that people will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection.
The claim that only worldly life exists and that people will not be resurrected gives a direct contrary formulation.
Observing how God originates creation and then repeats it directly frames renewed creation as easy for God.
The certainty that every soul tastes death and returns to God supplies the return dimension absent from merely material imagery.
God begins creation and then repeats it before people are returned to Him, closely answering the focus's question.
Bringing living from dead and dead from living, then bringing the earth to life, establishes recurring life-from-death power.
The one who originated creation and repeats it makes repetition a direct argument for the possibility of return.
Creating and resurrecting all humanity as one soul counters any inference that the scale of ancestral return is impossible.
The objection that people will be lost in the earth and then recreated captures the focus's concern with bodily dissolution.
Death followed by return to the Lord provides the authoritative answer to the preceding denial.
God revives dead land by rain and explicitly says that the resurrection is like this.
Giving life to the dead establishes the central divine action behind the disputed emergence.
Dead earth revived and producing grain gives a recurring visible analogy for life after death.
The trumpet scene has people emerging from graves to their Lord, directly depicting the questioned outcome.
The question of who gives life to decayed bones is the closest explicit counterpart to the focus's appeal to dust.
The answer that the first Creator gives those bones life directly resolves the objection.
The Creator of the heavens and earth is affirmed able to create people again, broadening the answer to renewed creation.
The confession of two deaths and two lives recognizes repeated divine enlivening after death.
God gives life and causes death, and His command makes what He wills come to be, grounding resurrection in divine power.
Dead earth stirred and growing after water is expressly compared to God's giving life to the dead.
The materialist claim that only time destroys people states a neighboring form of the focus's denial.
God gives life, causes death, and gathers people for the Day of Resurrection beyond doubt.
The Creator of heaven and earth is affirmed able to give life to the dead, directly answering the denial.
The objection that death and dust make return unlikely is an especially close verbal and conceptual parallel to the focus.
Rain revives dead land, followed by the explicit statement that such is the coming forth.

The subsequent creation is declared God's responsibility, directly supporting renewed creation.

Knowledge of the first creation is offered so that people may remember the possibility of being recreated.

Being spread across the earth and then gathered to God supplies a collective return corresponding to the focus's plural speakers and fathers.

God's ability to restore even fingertips intensifies the answer to doubts about reassembly.
The one who creates from a drop is affirmed able to give life to the dead, linking original generation to resurrection.
The trumpet day when people come in crowds depicts the mass emergence that the focus doubts.

The earth's being leveled prepares the eschatological disclosure of what it contains.
The earth casts out what is within it, directly contributing an emergence-from-earth image.
God is explicitly declared able to return the human being, a concise direct assertion against impossibility.

The earth's exposure and the gathering of every person depict the comprehensive return that the focus doubts.

God gives life to the dead and has power over all things, directly asserting the power disputed in the focus.
God's possession of life and death supplies a broad divine-power foundation for return after death.
The Lord of east and west is affirmed fully able to replace people, extending the argument from creation to re-creation.
His ability to substitute others without being overcome reinforces the power to create anew.
